# A first 10k: a 10-week plan (active start)

*Generated by the Don't Die Retired guidance engine on 13 November 2026 from 38 sourced statements. Draft for review: not yet checked by a coach, physiotherapist or doctor.*

## The challenge

10 km (6.2 miles) of running, or running and walking. [1, 2]

**Before this plan:** If you cannot yet run for 20 minutes without stopping, do the NHS Couch to 5K first, or start with Great Run's run-walk plan. [3, 4, 5]

## Before you start

- If you have a health condition or are worried about your health, speak to your GP (family doctor) before you start training. [4, 6]
- Start from your current level and build up gradually; repeating a week is fine and is part of the plan, not a failure. [3, 4, 5]
- If you are new to running, give yourself 8 to 12 weeks to get ready for a 10k rather than 6, and if time is short use a run-walk approach. [7, 8]

## How the plan works

- Do most of your training at an easy, conversational effort, about 2 to 3 out of 10, where you could hold a full conversation. Keep a small share for harder work. [9, 10, 11, 12]
- Increase your training a little at a time. Big week-to-week jumps (more than about 30 per cent) were linked with more overuse injuries in a study of 874 new runners; the familiar 10 per cent rule is a sensible cap but is not firmly proven. [4, 13, 14]
- Every third or fourth week, ease back on volume to let your body absorb the work before building again; older runners and people under other stress may do best with every third week. [11, 15]
- Build one long session a week at an easy effort, growing towards the length and duration of the challenge itself. [2, 11, 16]
- Know the real demands of your challenge (distance, total climb, time on your feet, altitude) and make sure your plan builds towards them. [1, 2]
- Plan rest days into every week, and take an easier day when your legs are heavy. [4, 11, 17]
- Do strength exercises for the whole body on at least two days a week. In trials, strength training cut sports injuries to about a third. [2, 3, 5, 18, 19, 20]
- In the final two weeks, cut your training volume by roughly 40 to 60 per cent while keeping the same number of sessions and some of the same effort, so you arrive fresh. [11, 16, 21, 22, 23]
- Run at least three times a week, with rest days in between; beginner plans from the NHS and from Great Run both start with three runs a week. [4, 14, 23]

## Week by week

Rest on Mondays and Fridays. Strength and balance (about 30 minutes, routine below) on Wednesdays and Sundays. Why each part is there, and what changes each week, follows the table. The Saturday long run is the key session: at an easy pace; it is about time, not distance, and walking breaks are fine.

| Week | Tue | Thu | Sat: long run | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | easy run, 25 min | easy run, 25 min | 30 minutes |  |
| 2 | easy run, 25 min | easy run, 25 min | 35 minutes |  |
| 3 | easy run, 25 min | easy run, 25 min | 25 minutes | easier week |
| 4 | easy run, 25 min | easy run, 25 min | 35 minutes |  |
| 5 | easy run, 25 min | easy run, 25 min | 40 minutes |  |
| 6 | easy run, 25 min | easy run, 25 min | 35 minutes | easier week |
| 7 | easy run, 25 min | easy run, 25 min | 45 minutes |  |
| 8 | easy run, 25 min | easy run, 25 min | 50 minutes |  |
| 9 | easy run, 25 min | easy run, 25 min | 30 minutes | taper begins: same sessions, less of each |
| 10 | easy run, 20 min | rest | **the challenge** | event week: rest, sleep, eat well |

## What each part of the plan is for

- **The Saturday long run.** The long session prepares you for the length of the day itself. Its pace does not matter; covering the time or distance does, so keep it at a conversational effort. [1, 2, 11]
- **The easy runs.** Easy sessions add fitness without leaving you too tired for the long session. Top endurance athletes do about four in five of their sessions at this low effort. [9, 10]
- **Strength and balance.** Strength and balance work is what keeps you in one piece. In trials it cut sports injuries to about a third, it is part of the official guidance for everyone on at least two days a week, and core and balance work helps on rough ground. [2, 3, 18]
- **Rest days.** Rest days are when your body recovers from the work and adapts to it. The NHS's beginner running plan puts a rest day between every run. [4, 15]
- **Easier weeks.** An easier week every third week lets the tiredness of the previous weeks clear, so your fitness can rebound before you build again. [11, 15]
- **The taper.** Cutting back in the final weeks lets your muscles recover and your body refuel, so you arrive fresh rather than tired. In research, a two-week taper improved performance. [21, 22]

## Each week, and why

**Week 1: setting the pattern.**

- Five sessions and two rest days. The long run starts at 30 minutes.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 11]
- Tuesday's easy run: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [9, 10]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 18]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 15]

**Week 2: building.**

- The long run grows to 35 minutes, up from 30 minutes in your last full week.
- Why only this much more: big jumps from one week to the next are linked with overuse injuries. [4, 13, 14]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 18]

**Week 3: an easier week.**

- The long run eases back to 25 minutes.
- Why ease off: it lets the last two weeks' tiredness clear so your fitness can catch up [11, 15]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 15]

**Week 4: building.**

- The long run grows to 35 minutes, up from 35 minutes in your last full week.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 11]
- Tuesday's easy run: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [9, 10]

**Week 5: building.**

- The long run grows to 40 minutes, up from 35 minutes in your last full week.
- Why only this much more: big jumps from one week to the next are linked with overuse injuries. [4, 13, 14]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 18]

**Week 6: an easier week.**

- The long run eases back to 35 minutes.
- Why ease off: it lets the last two weeks' tiredness clear so your fitness can catch up [11, 15]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 15]

**Week 7: building.**

- The long run grows to 45 minutes, up from 40 minutes in your last full week.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 11]
- Tuesday's easy run: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [9, 10]

**Week 8: your biggest week.**

- Your longest long run of the plan, 50 minutes, as close to the real day as training gets.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 11]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 18]

**Week 9: taper.**

- The long run drops to 30 minutes, but you keep every session.
- Why less now: your muscles recover and your body refuels, so you arrive fresh [21, 22]
- Tuesday's easy run: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [9, 10]
- Keep both strength sessions but make them lighter: same sessions, less of each.
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 15]

**Week 10: the challenge.**

- Two short, easy outings early in the week and plenty of rest: your muscles recover and your body refuels, so you arrive fresh [21, 22]
- No strength sessions this week; arrive rested.


## Looking after your body

- Include balance work; for older adults the official guidance pairs it with strength on two days a week, the NHS says balance and flexibility work twice a week can reduce the risk of falling, and balance (proprioception) training also reduced injuries in trials. [3, 5, 18, 19, 20]
- Squat-type exercises are the backbone of leg and hip strength. Start with sit-to-stand and mini-squats, adding repetitions gradually, then move on to squats and lunges, with core work for balance on rough ground. [2, 24]
- Stretch after a long day if it feels good, but do not rely on stretching to prevent injury; trials found it made no difference, unlike strength and balance work. [2, 18]
- Weight-bearing activity such as walking and running helps keep bones strong. [3]
- If you have osteoporosis or a high risk of fractures, ask your GP (family doctor) whether high-impact exercise is right for you before adding it. [19]
- Exercise that challenges your balance and builds functional strength, progressed regularly and kept up over time, helps prevent falls as you get older; tai chi is another option. A review of 108 trials found exercise cut the rate of falls by about a quarter, and balance and functional exercises combined with strength work probably cut it by about a third. [25, 26, 27, 28]
- Keep a regular sleep routine through training, going to bed and getting up at around the same time each day; good sleep is part of recovery, and on multi-day trips a warm enough sleeping bag and mat matter more than people expect. [17, 22, 29]
- If you miss a session, do not worry about it; carry on with the plan, or repeat a week if you need to. [4, 22]

**Strength and balance routine (twice a week).** Squats, lunges, a core exercise such as a plank, and a balance exercise such as standing on one leg. Start with your own body weight, two sets of 8 to 12 slow repetitions, and add load only when that feels easy. [2, 3, 5, 18, 19, 20, 24]

## Fuel, drink and feet

- On long days eat regularly on the move, a little and often from a variety of foods, rather than one big meal before you start. [2, 30]
- Use your long sessions to practise exactly what you will eat and drink on the day, building up gradually so your stomach gets used to it. Nothing new on the day. [22, 30]
- Train in the footwear you will use on the day and break new shoes in gradually. Wear moisture-wicking socks and change them if your feet sweat. [17, 22, 31]
- Deal with a hot spot as soon as you feel it. Cover a blister with a soft or padded plaster and do not burst it; get advice if it shows signs of infection. [17, 31]

## On the day

- Start slower than you think you need to; early miles feel easy and are where most people overdo it. [9, 22]
- Warm up for about 5 to 10 minutes before you run with moving exercises, such as marching on the spot, knee lifts and gentle knee bends, rather than held stretches. [14, 32]

## Safety

- If you have osteoporosis or a high risk of fractures, ask your GP (family doctor) whether high-impact exercise is right for you before adding it. [19]
- Drink when you are thirsty rather than to a schedule. Drinking far more than you need can dilute the body's sodium, which can be dangerous; it affects walkers and recreational exercisers as well as racers. [33]
- Call 999 (911 in the US) for tight or squeezing chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw, severe breathlessness, or if someone collapses. Do not drive yourself to hospital. [34]
- Stop if something does not feel right, and get it checked rather than training through it. [4, 22]
